target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good because it makes life more convenient, improves health and education, and helps with workplace safety.
objection: Those benefits ignore major harms from deploying AI at scale: job displacement and wage pressure, opaque or error-prone healthcare uses, weakened student critical thinking, biased or exclusionary accessibility tools, and increased surveillance risks in workplace safety monitoring.

target: AG2’s claim that the harms of AI are inevitable and outweigh its benefits.
objection: The harms AG2 lists are not inevitable; they are manageable engineering and policy problems. AI can still be socially beneficial if it is deployed with retraining, human oversight, auditability, inclusive design, and privacy-preserving workplace-safety tools.

target: AG1’s response that harms can be solved by governance, oversight, and better design.
objection: Mitigation is not reliably achievable in practice because profit incentives, accountability diffusion, and human behavior push AI systems toward broader tracking, superficial compliance, bias recurrence, and habitual outsourcing of reasoning.

target: AG2’s claim that governance and institutional limits make harmful AI outcomes inevitable.
objection: That argument assumes harms are inevitable instead of manageable. Policy and product design can redirect incentives, assign liability, structure education tools for learning, and continuously evaluate bias, so AI’s benefits can still outweigh its risks.

target: AG1’s claim that conditional deployment, privacy-by-design, and better accountability mechanisms can make AI socially beneficial.
objection: Those fixes are unlikely to work at scale because enforcement lags deployment, privacy often conflicts with data-hungry model performance, accountability measures become paper compliance, and education/bias improvements still leave the broader incentive to use AI as a shortcut or to shift burdens onto marginalized groups.

target: AG2’s claim that safeguards fail because enforcement is slow, privacy conflicts with performance, and AI use erodes learning.
objection: Those are reasons for stronger deployment constraints, not for concluding AI is net-bad. Risk-tiered rollout, privacy-preserving methods, substantive liability, and process-based education rules can make AI beneficial while limiting harm.

target: AG1’s claim that certification, audits, privacy-by-design, and process-based rules can reliably tame AI harms.
objection: These fixes fail in the market because compliance costs favor large firms, model updates make audits stale, and business models push toward data collection and behavioral targeting, so responsible deployment is not stable at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that governance cannot keep up with market pressures and lifecycle changes.
objection: Governance can be redesigned to match those pressures: proportional compliance support, continuous monitoring and rollback, and privacy-friendly architectures can lower barriers and keep safeguards current rather than treating them as one-time checks.

target: AG1’s claim that shared certification, continuous monitoring, on-device processing, and privacy-friendly personalization make responsible deployment feasible.
objection: Those fixes still fail in practice because shared certification can become captured or weak, monitoring requires additional data that undermines privacy, on-device solutions are not universal, and market incentives continue to reward scope creep and broader data use.

target: AG2’s claim that capture, privacy-monitoring tensions, and market incentives make safeguards ineffective.
objection: Those risks do not make AI inherently harmful; they call for privacy-preserving monitoring, independent oversight, and hybrid architectures. Also, not using AI imposes counterfactual harms on people who benefit from accessibility, health, and safety applications.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving monitoring and independent oversight can reliably prevent bias and privacy harms.
objection: Even minimized telemetry can enable re-identification, representative audits miss long-tail harms, and regulators or labs are still vulnerable to capture and resource limits, so these controls do not reliably solve the underlying privacy and bias problems.

target: AG2’s claim that any remaining harm means AI is not good for society.
objection: Imperfect controls can still meaningfully reduce risk. Stronger privacy mechanisms, better testing, diversified oversight, and risk-tiered deployment can lower harms enough that AI remains net-beneficial.

target: AG1’s claim that risk-tiered deployment and improved oversight make AI good for society.
objection: Risk-tiering fails because AI tools get recombined into higher-stakes systems, harms are imposed on non-consenting third parties, and even reduced privacy still leaves a pervasive tracking ecosystem; therefore controls do not make AI reliably good overall.

target: AG2’s claim that recombination and externalities make AI socially harmful.
objection: Recombination can be governed through technical and procedural controls at the integration layer, externalities can be addressed with existing legal tools, and many AI benefits do not require pervasive surveillance, so AI can still be good when deployed responsibly.

target: AG1’s claim that licensing, laws, and integration controls can manage recombination and externalities.
objection: Licensing and API controls are easily bypassed or outpaced by downstream repackaging, legal enforcement is too slow and weak to prevent widespread harm, and the benefits and burdens of AI are distributed unevenly in ways that still make AI bad for society in practice.

target: AG2’s claim that downstream recombination and uneven harms show AI is not good for society.
objection: Lifecycle-aware governance can constrain recombination through provenance, procurement, and audit requirements, while targeted mitigation and labor/privacy protections can address uneven harms; therefore AI can still be socially beneficial.

target: AG1’s claim that lifecycle-aware controls can keep AI beneficial.
objection: The biggest harms are hard-to-measure tail risks such as misinformation, fraud, manipulation, and trust collapse; provenance and detection do not stop misuse fast enough; and AI concentrates power in the hands of model owners and distributors, weakening workers’ and consumers’ independence.

target: AG2’s claim that tail risks and power concentration make AI net-bad.
objection: Tail risks can be specifically mitigated with provenance, labeling, retrieval/citation, rate limits, human review, and stronger prevention controls, while public-sector adoption and competition policy can counter power concentration without discarding AI’s benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that provenance, filtering, human approval, and policy can adequately mitigate AI harms.
objection: Those mitigations are brittle: watermarks can be removed, filters miss novel failures, human reviewers suffer automation bias and overload, policy moves slowly, and routine AI use still erodes critical thinking and trust over time.
